---
title: "Post-training"
subtitle: "How a pretrained model becomes an assistant that follows instructions, and what that does and does not change"
---

*Prerequisites: the idea that a model has parameters adjusted by training,
and that a prompt is inference-time context rather than training.
`learn/training.qmd` covers the first; `learn/tokens-context.qmd` the
second. Both are linked where they matter, and neither is assumed.*

## 1. The gap pretraining leaves

Pretraining, as `learn/training.qmd` describes, adjusts a model's
parameters so that it assigns higher probability to the next token in a
very large body of text. That objective produces broad linguistic and
task capability, and a pretrained model given an instruction will often
continue it sensibly, because instructions followed by answers occur in
text. But nothing in the objective is aimed at the interaction a user
actually wants. A raw pretrained model is not specifically optimized to
read a request as an instruction rather than as text to continue, to
answer in the form the user needs, to decline or redirect some kinds of
requests, to prefer one acceptable answer over another, or to keep to
conversational norms consistently. Given "Explain the bridge closure",
it may explain it, or continue with more headlines, or produce a list of
similar prompts, because all of those follow such a sentence somewhere
in the training text.

The methods that close this gap are collectively called post-training.
They deliberately shape the model's behavior toward the interaction
patterns its builders want.

## 2. What post-training is

Post-training is additional parameter-updating training applied after
pretraining to shape the model's behavior, capabilities, preferences, or
safety characteristics. [S-55] The one invariant that matters most in
this course is in that sentence: post-training changes the model's
parameters. It is training in exactly the sense of the previous page,
with different data and, sometimes, different objectives, and when it is
finished the model is a different function than it was before.

That invariant separates post-training from a set of things it is often
confused with. A system prompt, the instructions a product places in
front of a conversation, is inference-time context. So is the
conversation itself, retrieved text, the definitions of any tools the
model may call, the results those tools return, and any memory or files
that surrounding software supplies to a call. None of these change a
single parameter. They change what the model is conditioning on for the
current call, and they are gone from the model the moment the call ends,
whatever the surrounding software chooses to store. [S-31] The rest of
this page is about the methods that do change parameters; the next page,
`learn/agents.qmd`, is largely about the things that do not.

## 3. Supervised instruction tuning

The simplest post-training idea is to show the model what a good
interaction looks like. The training data consists of pairs: an
instruction or prompt, and a response someone judged to be the desired
one. A tiny example:

> **Instruction:** "In one sentence, why was the bridge closed?"
>
> **Desired response:** "The bridge was closed because the traffic data
> showed a structural risk that needed inspection."

The model is trained on these pairs using the same language-model loss
as pretraining: the negative log-likelihood of the response tokens given
the instruction (the loss `learn/training.qmd` §3 defines). The
parameters are adjusted so that, given such an instruction, the
demonstrated kind of response becomes more probable. This is
**supervised fine-tuning**, or instruction tuning when the pairs are
instructions and answers. In the InstructGPT work that made the recipe
widely known, the first stage was exactly this: a dataset of
labeler-written demonstrations of desired behavior, used to fine-tune a
pretrained model with supervised learning. [S-46]

Instruction tuning does not guarantee compliance or correctness. It
raises the probability of responses that resemble the demonstrations,
and a model that has seen a few thousand good answers can still produce
a bad one on a new prompt. What it changes is the default: after
instruction tuning, "Explain the bridge closure" is far more likely to
be treated as a request for an explanation than as a headline to
continue.

## 4. Why demonstrations are not enough

For many prompts there is no single correct string to demonstrate. Two
answers to "What should the agency do about the bridge?" may both be
reasonable, and a reviewer may still prefer one because it is more
helpful, more relevant, clearer, safer, better organized, or less likely
to mislead. Writing one demonstration per prompt throws that information
away, and writing the single best answer for every prompt is expensive
and often impossible.

The conceptual change that addresses this is small but important.
Instead of only showing the model a target response, one can collect
information about which of several responses is preferred. In many
settings, asking a reviewer to compare two candidate answers ("A is
better than B") can be easier or cheaper than asking the reviewer to
write an ideal answer from scratch; a comparison captures information
about relative preference that a single demonstration does not; and
comparisons can be collected on the model's own outputs, which is where
its mistakes actually appear.

## 5. Preference-based post-training

Post-training on preferences is a family of methods sharing one setup:
generate candidate responses to prompts; collect judgments about which
candidates are preferred; use those judgments to update the model's
parameters toward the preferred behavior. The members of the family
differ in how the last step is carried out. [S-55]

**The reward-model and reinforcement-learning route.** The pipeline
usually called RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback, works
in two stages. Terminology here is not perfectly standardized; some
writers use "RLHF" for any preference-based post-training. This page uses
"classic RLHF pipeline" or "RLHF-style" for this specific route. First,
the comparison data is used to train a separate
**reward model**, a network that takes a prompt and a response and
outputs a single score predicting how a human rater would rank it.
Second, the language model is updated by reinforcement learning to
produce responses that score highly under the reward model, while being
constrained not to drift too far from the model it started from.
InstructGPT's second stage followed this route: rankings of model
outputs were collected and used to fine-tune the supervised model with
reinforcement learning from human feedback. [S-46] The constraint is not
decoration. The reward model is an imperfect stand-in for human
judgment, and a model optimized hard against it will find responses that
score well without being good; keeping the updated model close to its
starting point limits how far that can go. If it helps to see the shape
of this particular route (it is a schematic of the classic RLHF pipeline,
not a definition of post-training or of preference optimization in
general), the quantity being maximized is roughly

$$
\text{expected reward} \;-\; \beta \times \text{(divergence from the reference model)}
$$

where $\beta$ sets how strongly drift is penalized. The details of the
reinforcement-learning algorithm used to do the maximizing are beyond
this page; the two-term structure is what matters. The InstructGPT
authors reported that outputs from their 1.3-billion-parameter
post-trained model were preferred by raters to outputs from the
175-billion-parameter pretrained model, while noting that the
post-trained model still made simple mistakes. [S-46]

**The direct preference optimization route.** The two-stage pipeline is
complex to run: it requires a separate reward model and repeated
sampling from the language model during training. Direct preference
optimization (DPO) and related methods reach a similar goal by a
shorter path. They rewrite the same constrained objective so that, given
a fixed preference dataset, the language model can be updated directly
from the comparison pairs, using a loss that resembles ordinary
classification, without training a separate reward model and without the
online, reward-model-guided reinforcement-learning loop of the classic
pipeline. (The preference dataset itself may well have been built by
sampling candidate responses; what DPO removes is the separate reward
model and that optimization loop.) [S-47] Its
authors reported that it matched or improved on the reward-model route
on the tasks they tested, while being substantially simpler to run.
[S-47] That is a result for those experiments, not a general verdict;
both routes remain in use, and providers mix and vary them.

The takeaway is a distinction in kind. Preference learning is a goal
and a family; RLHF-style and DPO-style methods are different
implementations of it. "RLHF" names one route through the family, not
the family, and not post-training as a whole.

## 6. Human feedback is not the only feedback

The judgments in §5 do not have to come from people. Preference or
critique signals can be produced or assisted by models, by written
rules, by automatic verifiers, or by other processes. One published
example is Constitutional AI, in which the human oversight is a written
list of principles. In its supervised phase, an initial model's
responses are critiqued and revised by the model itself against those
principles, and the original model is fine-tuned on the revised
responses. In its reinforcement-learning phase, a model judges which of
two responses is better, a preference model is trained on that dataset
of AI preferences, and the language model is then trained with the
preference model as the reward signal, which its authors call
reinforcement learning from AI feedback. [S-48]

The point of this section is narrow. It is not that every provider uses
this method, and not that human feedback is obsolete. It is that the
equation "post-training = humans rank answers = one particular
reinforcement-learning algorithm" is false on every term. The source of
the feedback, the form it takes, and the algorithm that consumes it are
three separate choices.

## 7. Reinforcement learning and reasoning-oriented training

Reinforcement learning, used in §5 and §6 as one route for preference
data, is a broad optimization framework: behavior is updated using a
reward signal computed on what the model produced, rather than by
matching a fixed target string. Anything that can be scored can, in
principle, supply the reward.

A more recent use applies that observation to tasks whose outcomes can
be checked automatically. If a mathematics problem has a known answer,
or a program has tests, a response can be rewarded for being correct
without any rater and without a learned reward model. Reinforcement
learning against such rewards can then incentivize whatever behavior
raises the reward, including producing longer intermediate reasoning
before the final answer and checking that answer before committing to
it.

The public case that established this is documented in the DeepSeek-R1
report, and its two models must be kept apart. DeepSeek-R1-Zero was
trained by what the report calls pure reinforcement learning, without
supervised fine-tuning as a preliminary step, using rule-based rewards
for accuracy and format rather than a neural reward model on reasoning
tasks. The report describes the model's responses growing steadily
longer over training, with self-verification and reflection appearing
in them, and it reports strong results on verifiable tasks; it also
reports that R1-Zero suffered from poor readability and mixing of
languages within a response. DeepSeek-R1 is a different model, trained
through a multi-stage framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning,
rejection sampling, and reinforcement learning, precisely to address
those problems. [S-49] Describing DeepSeek-R1 as "pure RL" conflates the
two, and generalizing either recipe to every reasoning-oriented model is
unsupported: other providers have published less, and recipes differ.

Two cautions apply to the reasoning traces such models produce. On some
difficult tasks, producing intermediate reasoning tokens provides
additional inference-time computation and can improve performance; that
is the supported statement. [S-49] It does not follow that the generated
text is a faithful transcript of the model's internal computation, or
that it is thought in the human sense; the tokens are output, produced
by the same next-token mechanism as any other output. The policy was
optimized using outcome and format reward signals; the intermediate text
was not supervised as a faithful description of the model's internal
computation. Saying that a model "needs tokens to think" is
shorthand for the first statement, not a technical claim about the
second.

## 8. Post-training does not replace pretraining

Every method above starts from a pretrained model and changes it
further. Many broad language and task capabilities, the ability to write
fluent text on nearly any topic, to follow the shape of an argument, to
produce code, are established during pretraining, and post-training
begins from that pretrained model and further changes its behavior and
capabilities: how those capabilities are elicited, what the model does
by default when given an instruction, a preference-laden choice, or a
checkable problem, and, as §5 and §7 show, how well it performs on some
tasks.

A tidy slogan is available here and should be refused: "pretraining
creates intelligence, post-training creates personality." It is wrong in
both directions. Post-training can measurably change task performance,
as §5 and §7 show, not only tone; and the behaviors post-training shapes,
such as answering rather than continuing, were already present in the
pretrained model as possibilities, not absent from it. The mechanistic
statement is the accurate one: pretraining and post-training are both
parameter updates, on different data, with different objectives, and
the finished model is the result of both.

## 9. Model versus assistant

The word "model" in this course means a parameterized neural network
that maps inference-time context to a probability distribution over the
next token. Post-training changes that network. An **assistant**, the
thing a person actually types to, is a product built around a model, and
it usually adds a great deal that is not in the network: a system prompt
carrying instructions and a persona; management of the conversation
state; retrieval of documents; tools the model may request; safety
checks applied before or after the model call; a user interface; and
other product logic that decides what enters the context and what
leaves it. [S-31]

The assistant is therefore not identical to the underlying model, and
its behavior can be changed in two entirely different ways. Post-training
changes the model. Changing the system prompt, adding a tool, enabling
retrieval, or altering the product logic changes the assistant's
behavior without touching a parameter. Two assistants built on the same
post-trained model can behave quite differently, and the same assistant
can behave differently tomorrow after a system-prompt change with no
training run in between. `learn/agents.qmd` builds on exactly this
separation.

## 10. Common misconceptions

**"Post-training means RLHF."** RLHF is one route through one family of
post-training methods. Supervised instruction tuning, direct preference
optimization, AI-generated feedback, and reinforcement learning against
automatic checks are all post-training too, and recipes combine them
differently (§3–§7).

**"A system prompt is post-training."** A system prompt is inference-time
context. It changes what the model conditions on for a call and changes
no parameter (§2).

**"The assistant and the model are the same thing."** The assistant is
a product around the model. Much of its behavior comes from instructions,
tools, retrieval, and product logic that never touch the model's
parameters (§9).

**"Reasoning models were trained simply by asking for a chain of
thought."** Asking for intermediate reasoning in a prompt is
inference-time context, not parameter-updating training. In the DeepSeek
R1 and R1-Zero case discussed here, reinforcement learning against
checkable rewards was central to the training recipe, with R1 using a
multi-stage process. Other reasoning-oriented models may use different
recipes, and many providers do not publish enough detail to characterize
them this specifically (§7).

## 11. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Pretraining and post-training both change the model's
parameters. What differs between them?</summary>
The data and the objective. Pretraining maximizes next-token likelihood
on a very large general corpus. Post-training uses much smaller sets of
demonstrations, preference comparisons, or checkable tasks, with
objectives chosen to shape behavior, and starts from the pretrained
parameters rather than from scratch (§2, §8).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A dataset contains pairs of responses to the same prompt with a
label saying which one a reviewer preferred. Is this supervised
instruction tuning?</summary>
No. Instruction tuning trains on a single demonstrated response per
prompt. Comparison labels are preference data, and they are used by
preference-based methods, whether through a reward model and
reinforcement learning or through a direct method such as DPO (§4–§5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Does DPO use the same reward-model-plus-reinforcement-learning
pipeline as classic RLHF?</summary>
No. DPO uses preference comparisons to update the language model directly
and does not require that separate reward-model-plus-online-RL pipeline.
Both are members of the same family, preference-based post-training; they
differ in mechanism (§5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>A company changes its assistant's system prompt so that it
answers more concisely. Has the model been post-trained?</summary>
No. The system prompt is inference-time context. The assistant's
behavior changed; the model's parameters did not (§2, §9).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>Two products use the same post-trained model but behave
differently. Does that contradict anything on this page?</summary>
No. The assistant is the model plus instructions, conversation state,
retrieval, tools, safety checks, and product logic. Those can differ
between products while the model, and its parameters, are identical
(§9).
</details>
:::

## 12. Continue learning

- **Ouyang et al., *Training language models to follow instructions with
  human feedback*** (paper, arXiv:2203.02155; the abstract and Section 3
  describe the three-stage recipe). Technical level. The primary source
  for the supervised-then-reward-model-then-RL pipeline, with the
  striking size comparison quoted in §5. Limitation: one provider's 2022
  recipe; current recipes vary.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155>

- **Rafailov et al., *Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model
  is Secretly a Reward Model*** (paper, arXiv:2305.18290; the
  introduction is enough for the idea). Technical level, with a
  derivation for those who want it. Especially good for seeing why the
  reward-model stage can be folded away. Limitation: the comparison
  results are for the tasks and scales tested in the paper.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290>

- **Bai et al., *Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback***
  (paper, arXiv:2212.08073; the abstract states the two phases).
  Technical level. The primary source for feedback generated by a model
  under written principles. Limitation: describes one method at one
  provider in 2022.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073>

- **DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in
  LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*** (paper, arXiv:2501.12948; the
  abstract and introduction distinguish R1-Zero from R1). Technical
  level. The most detailed public account of reinforcement learning
  against checkable rewards producing long reasoning traces. Limitation:
  one lab's recipe; the reasoning traces it shows should not be read as
  transcripts of internal computation.
  <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>

course, with full source-map entries.
